title: The Ramgarhia misl
hookLine: Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, a carpenter's son, whose towers still stand at the Harmandir

cards: A carpenter's son rides with the Khalsa. Tradition says his family worked with wood and tools, and that he grew up knowing how a thing is put together, joint by joint. Riding didn't stop him being a builder.
He built a fort. And beside the Harmandir in Amritsar, towers linked to his name still stand. His name was Jassa Singh, the same as yesterday's chief, and people told the two apart by their bands.

teach.h: RAM RAUNI: A MUD FORT BY AMRITSAR.
teach.b: How a band got its name from a building. First, a mud fort. Tradition says that in the hard years, Sikhs raised a small fort of earth near Amritsar and called it Ram Rauni, after Guru Ram Das, who founded the city.
It was a place to stand and hold out when the city was threatened. Second, the builder.

Tradition says Jassa Singh rebuilt and strengthened it, and it was renamed Ramgarh, Ram's fort. The men who held it became the Ramgarhias, the band of Ramgarh, and their leader became Jassa Singh Ramgarhia.
Not a village, not a nickname: a thing built and built again. Third, the towers.

Beside the Harmandir stands the Ramgarhia Bunga, tall towers Sikh tradition links to Jassa Singh and his misl. A bunga is a building near the Harmandir where Sikhs could stay and, in the hard years, keep watch.
From the top, you could see who was coming. The towers are still there, in the same complex. Fourth, the name that stayed.
Ramgarhia came to be used more widely for Sikhs of carpenter and craftsman families, some of whom were proud to share Jassa Singh's name.
A craftsman's son led riders, and the craftsmen kept his name.

how: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ramgarhia in Sikh histories, and pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib can see the Ramgarhia Bunga's towers in the same complex.

o: Ram's fort near Amritsar, rebuilt by Jassa Singh

games.q: the builder's band — tap the pairs.

s: the Ramgarhia misl was named for a village
it was named for Ramgarh, the fort near Amritsar.
the Ramgarhia Bunga stands near the Harmandir
its towers are in the same complex today.
there was only one Jassa Singh among the misl chiefs
Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Jassa Singh Ramgarhia rode in the same years.

games.q: you're a carpenter's son riding with the Khalsa. the little mud fort near Amritsar is weak. what do you do?
o: leave it; forts are for kings.
games.why: tradition says Jassa Singh rebuilt it, it was renamed Ramgarh, and his band became the Ramgarhias.

practice: Find one made thing near you, a chair, a door frame, a mug, the stitching on your sleeve, and let your eyes rest on it.
Notice how it's joined and where someone took care, an edge sanded smooth, a seam that holds, staying with one detail per breath. If you pray, let Waheguru go out with each breath.

wordCard.voice: Ramgarh, Ram's fort at Amritsar, rebuilt and renamed by Jassa Singh, the fort that gave the Ramgarhia misl its name. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for Ramgarhia: 'of Ramgarh', Ram's fort at Amritsar.

carryVoice: Your line: the builder's misl. Someone's hands made every joint. Eight hundred ninety days now.
